questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.topic: Presumption of constitutionality
questions.learningObjective: Explain how the presumption of constitutionality allocates the burden of proof
questions.stem: Seeing-log line 21 - my friend asked why a state statute that survives ordinary review still begins with a strong presumption of validity.

answer.exemplar: A law is presumed valid until the party challenging it shows that it violates the Constitution, so the challenger bears the burden and the government need only defend the law after a challenge is raised. The presumption is rebuttable rather than a shield, because it allocates the burden of proof rather than deciding the outcome.

questions.explanation: The presumption shifts the burden to whoever attacks the law, and it disappears once a serious challenge is made. It is a starting point for the litigation, not an immunity from review.
questions.hint: Ask who must carry the burden of proof.

questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.topic: Why levels are treated differently
questions.learningObjective: Explain why reviewing courts apply different standards to different questions
questions.stem: Ridge notebook 7 - a friend asked why a trial court's finding of fact gets more deference than a legal conclusion drawn from the same record.

answer.exemplar: Trial courts hear the witnesses and weigh the evidence, so they are best placed to resolve disputed facts, and reviewing courts overturn factual findings only for clear error. Legal conclusions are treated differently because the reviewing court decides what the law is and applies it to the record itself, so those conclusions are reviewed without deference to the trial court.

questions.explanation: Factual findings depend on the record the trial court built, so reviewing courts defer unless the finding is clearly wrong. Questions of law are decided by the reviewing court, which applies the law to the record itself.
questions.hint: Ask what the reviewing court is best placed to do.

questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.topic: Why levels are treated differently
questions.learningObjective: Explain why reviewing courts apply different standards to different questions
questions.stem: Field note 40 - I asked why a federal court takes the state high court's answer on a state law question but decides federal law for itself.

answer.exemplar: A federal court must apply federal law itself, and it must also apply the state law that the state high court has authoritatively interpreted, since a federal court is bound by state law on state issues. The result is that on state questions the federal court follows the state high court, while on federal questions the federal court decides the matter independently.

questions.explanation: Federal courts must decide federal law for themselves but must apply state law as the state's highest court has construed it. That asymmetry explains why state holdings are followed while federal holdings are not.
questions.hint: Ask what each court is required to apply.

questions.stem: Observation 6 - my friend said a law must be struck down if he can think of one reason it might fail, and I said that is not how the presumption works.

answer.exemplar: Courts review economic and social regulation under the presumption that the law is valid, and the challenger must show that no conceivable set of facts supports the legislature's choice. A court does not reweigh the evidence or substitute its own judgment about wisdom; it asks only whether a rational basis exists for what the legislature did.

options.text: The fully permitted laundromat, because its owners still face competition.
options.misconception: invents a taking from ordinary competition

questions.explanation: Only the lakefront lot leaves no economically viable use, since nothing may be built there. A time limit and a use conversion both leave the owner free to operate something, so neither is a total taking.
questions.hint: Ask which parcel allows no use whatsoever.

questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.topic: Why levels are treated differently
questions.learningObjective: Explain why reviewing courts apply different standards to different questions
questions.stem: Sketchpad page 30 - I asked why a state court could hear some disputes over the federal Constitution while others belong in federal court.

answer.exemplar: Whether a federal court may hear a case turns on the source of the claim and the jurisdictional requirements, not on the importance of the issue. A dispute presenting a substantial federal question can often be brought in federal court on that basis, while a dispute arising between citizens of different states may be heard there on the basis of diversity. Otherwise, state courts remain the courts of first instance.

questions.explanation: Federal jurisdiction depends on a federal question or diversity, plus other statutory requirements. Importance and convenience play no part, so state courts remain the courts of first instance.
questions.hint: Ask what the jurisdictional requirement is.

questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.topic: Two grounds for refusing to decide
questions.learningObjective: Count the grounds on which a court may refuse to decide a state question
questions.stem: Field note 29 - my tally of eight orders refusing to decide a state question was: three citing an unsettled state question, three treating a federal constitutional issue as dispositive, and two dismissing for lack of a live controversy. How many orders relied on a ground other than the unsettled state question?
questions.explanation: The three orders finding a federal issue dispositive and the two dismissing for lack of a live controversy used other grounds, so 3 plus 2 equals 5. The three orders citing unsettled state law are excluded from the tally.
questions.hint: Exclude the unsettled state-law orders.

questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.topic: Which reading of a state rule governs
questions.learningObjective: Determine which reading of a state rule governs in a reviewing court

stimulus.body: Excerpt from state licensing guidance: for purposes of this rule, the phrase full-time resident means a person who has an address in the state and files an income tax return here. The guidance notes that a person may satisfy one of these conditions without the other, in which case the license application is not sufficient on its own.

questions.stem: Clearing skies at last, log 36 - I copied licensing guidance that defines a statutory phrase. Which statement about the governing reading is correct?

options.text: The guidance controls, so no further inquiry into the statutory text is needed.
options.misconception: makes guidance conclusive

options.text: The guidance has no weight, because only the legislature may define statutory terms.
options.misconception: denies any role for reasonable agency readings

options.text: The court must pick the reading that most applicants would prefer.
options.misconception: lets preference select the reading

options.text: A court gives the agency's reasonable reading deference, but only if the enacted text can bear it.

questions.explanation: A reasonable administrative reading of ambiguous state law receives deference, but it cannot go beyond what the enacted text allows. Here the text defines the phrase, so the guidance must fit it.
questions.hint: Ask whether the text supports the guidance.
